title: The day is short (Avot 2:15)
hook: Rabbi Tarfon: the day is short, the work is great, the workers are lazy

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Elazar: know what to answer the skeptic, and know before whom you toil. Your line was know before whom you toil. What hard question did you look into? Day two hundred sixty-three.

It's four in the afternoon. You look at your list. Somehow the easy things got done: the emails, the small errands, a very thorough reorganization of your desk. And the one hard thing, the thing that actually mattered, is still sitting at the top of the list, untouched. The light is already changing. Rabbi Tarfon, a priest who lived through the years when the Temple was destroyed, knew that four o'clock feeling. And he put it into five short phrases that sound like a foreman shouting across a building site.
screen: `FOUR IN THE AFTERNOON.` → `THE HARD THING, UNTOUCHED.` → `A FOREMAN ON A BUILDING SITE.`

segments.voice: Here's Rabbi Tarfon. The day is short. The work is great. The workers are lazy. The reward is great. And the master of the house is pressing. Start with the world he's describing. In ancient Israel, a day laborer worked from sunrise to sundown, and the Torah said he had to be paid before the sun went down. So the whole day has a clock on it. When the light's gone, it's gone. Now read the saying as a picture of a life. The day is short: a lifetime goes faster than anyone expects. The work is great: there's so much to learn, so much good to do, so many people who need something. The workers are lazy: that's us, honestly. Not wicked. Just distracted, tired, reorganizing the desk. The reward is great: the work is worth it, more than we can see. And the master of the house is pressing: God, in this picture, is the owner of the field, and there's a gentle urgency in the air. Notice what Rabbi Tarfon doesn't say. He doesn't say you're a failure, or it's hopeless. He just names the situation as plainly as a foreman would, and trusts you to do the math. If the day is short and the work is great, you start with the thing that matters most. And if this sounds like a lot of pressure, hold on. Tomorrow, the very next line of Pirkei Avot, from the same Rabbi Tarfon, lets you breathe again.
screen: `FIVE SHORT PHRASES.` · `PAID BEFORE SUNDOWN.` · `A LIFE IS A WORKING DAY.` · `START WITH WHAT MATTERS MOST.` · then, large: `THE DAY IS SHORT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Let today's list come to mind. Notice which item you keep circling around. The hard one. The one that matters. Don't feel guilty about it. Just see it clearly. Then picture the first five minutes of doing it, right after this. Where you'll sit. What you'll open. The first sentence, the first call, the first step. The bell holds the time.
The day is short. Rabbi Tarfon's five phrases: the day is short, the work is great, the workers are lazy, the reward is great, the master is pressing.
Your line: the day is short. Today, start the hard thing first, before the easy ones fill up the light. Day two hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Rabbi Tarfon's saying is often quoted in Jewish teaching as a reminder that life is brief and there is much good to do, and it is usually paired with the saying that follows it.

match.prompt: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.

myth: a day laborer in ancient Israel was paid before sundown
the Torah said he had to be paid that same day.
Rabbi Tarfon calls the workers wicked
he calls them lazy: distracted, tired, human.
Rabbi Tarfon lived through the time the Temple was destroyed
he was a priest, and served there as a young man.

fork.setup: it's four in the afternoon. the easy tasks are done and the hard one hasn't been touched. what does Rabbi Tarfon's saying suggest?
options: tidy a few more small things first.
start the hard thing now. the day is short.
leave it for tomorrow. there's always tomorrow.
fork.reveal: the day is short and the work is great, he says. if the light is going, start with what matters most.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: the day is short, and the work is great.

trapdoor: what it means: a life is a working day, brief and full of good work worth doing, so start with what matters.
what a scholar hears: the saying pictures a day laborer's world, where the Torah required wages paid before sundown.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Rabbi Tarfon 'wrote it down' changed to 'put it into' (the Mishnah records sayings; it does not say he wrote); 'Picture the world' reworded.
Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). Numbering: 2:15 common, 2:20 in some editions.
Rabbi Tarfon as a kohen who served in the Temple as a young man: Jerusalem Talmud Yoma 3:7 and Kiddushin 71a (he recalls standing on the dais with his priestly brothers); confirm.
Wages paid before sundown: Deuteronomy 24:15 (and Leviticus 19:13).
Identifying the 'master of the house' as God follows common commentary.
